title: Ethiopia and Eritrea on the brink
deck: Addis Ababa says Eritrean troops are inside Tigray, Asmara calls that a 'declaration of war', and a region already short of food and aid sits between two armies, a rebel alliance and the Red Sea's most sensitive shipping lane.

fuel.title: Army chief blames Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan
fuel.how: Ethiopia's army chief has widened the list of states Addis Ababa says back the TPLF, which raises the odds that a Tigray war becomes a regional one.

fuel.title: TPLF rejects new Tigray administration
fuel.how: The rebels' refusal to recognise the new regional administration keeps control of Tigray contested, so federal gains in the cities may not end the fighting.

fuel.title: WHO scales up Tigray emergency health response
fuel.how: About 4 million people in Tigray need urgent aid, and a wider war would push refugees and arms toward eastern Sudan and pull aid logistics away from Darfur.

fuel.title: Assab claims add Bab al-Mandeb risk
fuel.how: Eritrea says Addis Ababa wants to seize the port of Assab, which would add a second flashpoint to a Red Sea route already strained by the Iran war.

card.headline: Ethiopia and Eritrea are trading war accusations while Tigray burns and the Red Sea route waits

Distant, but the Red Sea lane carries freight and fuel. A second flashpoint there could feed prices that are already high.

Addis Ababa looks for outside backing, with Abiy's call to Netanyahu one sign.

whatHappened: On 9 October 2026 Ethiopia told the UN Security Council that Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 km into Tigray. It invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, the right to self-defence. On 10 October Eritrea replied that this was a 'declaration of war' and said Addis Ababa wants to seize the Red Sea port of Assab.

On the ground, federal forces retook the Tigrayan capital Mekelle on 3-4 October and the town of Adigrat on 10 October. They were fighting a seven-group rebel alliance led by the TPLF, formed in September. The two states had severed diplomatic ties on 1 October.

Since then, Ethiopia's army chief has accused Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan of backing the TPLF. The TPLF has rejected the new Tigray administration as illegitimate. Prime Minister Abiy spoke with Israel's Netanyahu on 25 October. Press accounts vary and many claims come from the warring parties, so treat them with care.
whyItMatters: Security: Ethiopia is the Horn's most populous state and Eritrea's army is large and battle-tested. Addis Ababa now publicly blames three neighbours for the Tigray fighting. That makes a misjudgement or a border clash more likely to spiral into a regional war.

Politics: Retaking Mekelle and Adigrat gives Addis Ababa a battlefield footing, but the TPLF's refusal to recognise the new Tigray administration means the political dispute is open. Federal military gains may not end the insurgency.

Displacement: Roughly 4 million people in Tigray need urgent aid. Our assessment is that a Tigray-Eritrea war would push refugees and arms into eastern Sudan and divert aid logistics from Darfur and Kordofan. There, an IPC alert of 12 October says famine risk is accelerating, with child acute malnutrition at 38% and 30.8% in two South Darfur camps.

Trade: Ships to and from the Red Sea pass the Bab al-Mandeb strait. The Iran war, which began on 28 February 2026, has kept oil and freight costs high for eight months. Eritrea's claim that Ethiopia wants Assab would, if it led to fighting, add a second risk to that approach.

winners.why: Wars in the region tend to increase demand for weapons, though we have no sourced figures here.

winners.who: Hardliners in Addis Ababa and Asmara
winners.why: External threats can justify tighter control at home. This is our judgement, not a sourced claim.
Egypt, Gulf states and Israel have interests in the Red Sea and Nile politics; Abiy's call to Netanyahu suggests Addis Ababa is shopping for support.

losers.why: About 4 million need urgent aid, and fighting in Mekelle, Adigrat and the border zone makes delivery harder.
Aid and donor attention may be diverted, and refugees and arms may flow into eastern Sudan, per the connection assessed for this report.

losers.who: Shippers and importers using the Red Sea
losers.why: A second chokepoint risk raises insurance and freight costs on top of the Iran-war shock.
A war economy, cut diplomatic ties and multiple internal conflicts raise risk and costs. Evidence here is thin, so this is a judgement.

whatsNext: Watch for any UN Security Council follow-up to the 9 October session and for African Union or Gulf mediation offers.
Watch whether federal forces consolidate in Tigray or whether the TPLF-led alliance mounts counterattacks.
Watch for fighting near Assab or the Eritrean border, which would signal a move from accusations to open interstate war.
Watch the humanitarian side: access to Tigray, WFP and WHO operations, and any flow of refugees toward Sudan.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what is the most likely path over the next six months?
options: Open Ethiopia-Eritrea war with fighting near Assab
Armed standoff, insurgency in Tigray and no formal talks
Wider regional war drawing in Sudan and Egypt
predict.explanation: Our base case, at about 45%, is an armed standoff. Accusations continue, Tigray stays contested, and neither capital chooses full war. The other paths are real: open war at about 20%, mediated de-escalation at about 25%, regional war at about 10%. These are author judgement.

timeline.title: Tigray war begins
timeline.detail: Federal forces fight the TPLF, with Eritrean troops widely reported to have joined the federal side. Hundreds of thousands died by some estimates; counts are uncertain.

timeline.title: Pretoria agreement ends the Tigray war
timeline.detail: The African Union-brokered deal stopped the fighting but left political and territorial disputes unresolved.

timeline.title: Strikes on Iran begin
timeline.detail: Oil and freight costs have stayed elevated for eight months, straining Red Sea routes and the region's economies.

timeline.title: TPLF-led seven-group rebel alliance forms
timeline.detail: Formed in September; the exact date is not given in the material, so this entry is approximate.

timeline.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea sever diplomatic ties
timeline.detail: The break removes the last formal channel between the two capitals.

timeline.title: Federal forces retake Mekelle
timeline.detail: Fighting for the Tigrayan capital took place on 3-4 October; the TPLF-led alliance is pushed out of its main city.

timeline.title: Ethiopia takes its case to the UN Security Council
timeline.detail: Addis Ababa says Eritrean troops advanced up to 60 km into Tigray and invokes Article 51.

timeline.title: Eritrea answers: 'declaration of war'
timeline.detail: Asmara says Ethiopia wants to seize Assab. Federal forces also retake Adigrat the same day.

timeline.title: Analysts warn of wider regional war
timeline.detail: The New Humanitarian reports fears that Eritrean incursions could widen the conflict; the IPC issues its Sudan famine alert the same day.

timeline.title: WHO scales up emergency health response
timeline.detail: Operations expand across Afar, Amhara and Tigray to meet needs from ongoing hostilities.

timeline.title: Army chief blames Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan; Abiy calls Netanyahu
timeline.detail: Ethiopia widens the circle of states it says back the TPLF, and the prime minister speaks to Israel's leader as tensions rise.

timeline.title: TPLF rejects new Tigray administration
timeline.detail: The rebels call the administration illegitimate, keeping the political dispute over Tigray open.

causes.name: Unfinished Tigray settlement
causes.detail: The 2022 Pretoria deal ended large-scale fighting but did not settle control of Tigray, the TPLF's role or Eritrea's position.

causes.name: Red Sea access
causes.detail: Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea's independence in 1993, and its leaders have talked about regaining sea access. Eritrea now says Assab is Addis Ababa's target.

causes.name: Rivalry between the two capitals
causes.detail: The two states fought a border war in 1998-2000 and made peace only in 2018. That peace has now collapsed.

causes.name: Rebel alliance forms
causes.detail: A TPLF-led seven-group alliance emerged in September, giving Addis Ababa a broader insurgent threat to answer.

causes.name: Diplomatic rupture
causes.detail: The two states severed ties on 1 October.

causes.name: Fighting for Tigray's cities
causes.detail: Federal forces retook Mekelle on 3-4 October and Adigrat on 10 October.

causes.name: Mutual accusations at the UN
causes.detail: Ethiopia invoked Article 51 and Eritrea called it a 'declaration of war'.

causes.name: Wider blame
causes.detail: The army chief also accuses Egypt and Sudan, which raises the stakes for neighbours.

causes.name: Disputed Tigray administration
causes.detail: The TPLF's refusal to accept the new administration keeps control contested.

causes.name: Strained regional economy
causes.detail: Eight months of Iran-war oil and freight costs leave governments and households with less room to absorb a new shock.

stakeholders.name: Abiy Ahmed and Ethiopia's federal government
stakeholders.role: Prime minister; claimant of Eritrean aggression
stakeholders.wants: Control of Tigray, defeat of the TPLF-led alliance and international backing for its case against Eritrea
stakeholders.leverage: Army, battlefield gains in Mekelle and Adigrat, UN diplomacy
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep pressing the Article 51 case, consolidate Tigray and seek outside backing, as the call to Netanyahu suggests

stakeholders.name: Isaias Afwerki and Eritrea
stakeholders.wants: To block any move on Assab and to protect its position in Tigray
stakeholders.leverage: Large, experienced army; control of its coast
stakeholders.likelyMove: Reject Ethiopian claims, signal readiness to fight, avoid concessions

stakeholders.name: TPLF and the seven-group alliance
stakeholders.wants: Recognition of its authority in Tigray and an end to the federal push
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep refusing the new administration and fight a mobile insurgency

stakeholders.name: Egypt and Sudan
stakeholders.role: Neighbours accused by Ethiopia's army chief
stakeholders.wants: Egypt: a counterweight to Ethiopia over Nile and Red Sea politics. Sudan: stability on its eastern border while its own war goes on
stakeholders.leverage: Border access, diplomatic and possibly material support (alleged, not proven)
stakeholders.likelyMove: Deny involvement while keeping options open

stakeholders.name: UN Security Council and African Union
stakeholders.leverage: Diplomatic cover, access to talks, aid
stakeholders.likelyMove: Hold sessions and call for restraint; real mediation is uncertain

stakeholders.name: Israel
stakeholders.role: Outside power in contact with Addis Ababa
stakeholders.leverage: Diplomacy and possibly security cooperation, though the material shows only a phone call

stakeholders.name: WHO, WFP and humanitarian agencies
stakeholders.wants: Safe access to Tigray, Afar and Amhara and funding
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep scaling health and food operations, appeal for money and access

sectors.why: Costs rise, not volumes: a second risk near Assab adds to the Iran-war strain on the Bab al-Mandeb approach.
Needs grow in Tigray, Afar and Amhara; the WHO is already scaling up. Funding is stretched across Sudan and Ethiopia.
War risk, cut diplomatic ties and multiple internal conflicts raise financing and operating costs. Evidence is thin and this is a judgement.
Governments and armed groups in the region are likely to want more weapons; no sourced figures yet.
Refugees and arms flows would stress already fragile areas, while cross-border trade could be disrupted.
Ethiopia could lean more on Djibouti if the Assab dispute worsens, but regional instability also raises risk there.
Importers face a further shock on top of elevated oil and freight costs; French diesel hit a record EUR 2.41 a litre in September.

dailyLife.effect: About 4 million people need urgent aid, and the WHO is expanding health operations across Afar, Amhara and Tigray.
Both towns changed hands in a matter of days; residents face uncertainty over who governs them.
Oil and freight costs have been elevated for eight months. Any added Red Sea risk would feed into import prices.
A wider war would likely push people toward eastern Sudan, where 8.58 million are already displaced nationwide.
With ties cut on 1 October, movement and communication between Ethiopia and Eritrea are limited.

scenarios.name: Armed standoff and Tigray insurgency
scenarios.looksLike: Both capitals trade accusations and move troops but avoid full war. Fighting continues inside Tigray; the TPLF-led alliance resists the new administration.
signposts: UN sessions with no mediation breakthrough
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Humanitarian needs grow, Red Sea risk premiums stay elevated and donor attention is split.

scenarios.name: Open Ethiopia-Eritrea war
scenarios.looksLike: Clashes near the border or Assab become sustained interstate fighting.
signposts: Fighting reported near Assab or the border
Mass troop movements or air strikes
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Red Sea shipping risk rises sharply; refugees and arms move toward Sudan; aid is diverted from Darfur.

scenarios.name: Mediated de-escalation
scenarios.looksLike: African Union, Gulf or UN mediation produces a ceasefire framework or restored contact.
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Risk premiums ease and aid access improves, though Tigray's political status stays unresolved.

scenarios.name: Regional spillover
scenarios.looksLike: Egypt, Sudan or other actors are drawn in, directly or through proxies.
signposts: Credible evidence of Egyptian or Sudanese support to the TPLF
scenarios.effectOnWorld: A multi-front Horn of Africa war with severe humanitarian and shipping consequences.

predictions.text: Ethiopia and Eritrea will not restore diplomatic ties (probability about 0.9).
A formal mediation or ceasefire process involving the African Union, UN or a regional power will be announced publicly (probability about 0.3).
Sustained direct fighting between Ethiopian and Eritrean forces, reported by at least two credible outlets, will occur (probability about 0.25).
The TPLF-led alliance will still control or contest significant territory in Tigray, so the federal government will not have fully pacified the region (probability about 0.7).
Humanitarian agencies will report that the number of Tigrayans needing urgent aid is no lower than 4 million (probability about 0.75).

actions: Add buffer time and war-risk insurance quotes to any lane through the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb.
Review exposure to Ethiopian and Eritrean suppliers and customers; identify single-source dependencies.
Add force-majeure and surcharge clauses to contracts touching the Horn of Africa.
Issue staff safety guidance for Ethiopia, especially Tigray, Afar and Amhara.
Treat Ethiopian sovereign and corporate risk as war risk until ties or talks resume.
Watch shipping and insurance costs on the Red Sea approach as a signal.
Do not assume a quick mediated settlement; the two states have cut ties and traded UN accusations.
Expect freight and fuel costs to stay elevated while the Iran war and Red Sea risks continue.
If you send money or travel to the region, check current advice and avoid Tigray and border areas.
If you donate, favour agencies working on Tigray and Sudan, where funding gaps are large.
Push for an urgent diplomatic channel between Addis Ababa and Asmara before a border incident escalates.
Protect humanitarian access to Tigray and keep Sudan's famine response funded separately.
Verify the allegations against Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan independently before acting on them.

analogues.whatFollowed: A costly conventional war with large casualties ended in an agreement, but the border dispute stayed unresolved for nearly two decades.
A war with Eritrean involvement caused enormous loss of life and displacement and ended with the Pretoria agreement, which left key political questions open.
A peace deal and a Nobel prize for Abiy in 2019 raised hopes, but the ties were never institutionalised; the 2026 rupture shows how fragile they were.

confidence.claim: Ethiopia told the UN on 9 October that Eritrean troops advanced up to 60 km into Tigray; Eritrea called it a 'declaration of war' on 10 October
confidence.note: Both statements are reported as made; the military claim itself is Ethiopia's and not independently verified here.

confidence.claim: Eritrean troops are actually inside Tigray at that depth
confidence.note: Comes from one party to the dispute; we have not seen independent verification.

confidence.claim: Federal forces retook Mekelle (3-4 October) and Adigrat (10 October)
confidence.note: From the event summary; an aggregator item dated 25 October repeats the Mekelle claim, suggesting later republication, so the dates may be imprecise.

confidence.claim: Ethiopia's army chief accuses Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan of backing the TPLF
confidence.note: Reported by Kulu Media and aggregators; the accusation is Ethiopia's, and the three states' roles are unproven.

confidence.claim: About 4 million people in Tigray need urgent aid
confidence.note: From the event summary; the WHO scale-up is separately sourced, but we did not check the 4 million figure against a primary UN document.

confidence.claim: Links to Sudan famine alert and Red Sea shipping risk
confidence.note: The connection is judged plausible by the editors; the actual size of refugee, arms or freight effects is estimated and not sourced.

evidence.method: Drafted from the listed sources and the headlines matched to this event, which run to 26 October 2026. Background on 1998-2000, 2018 and 2020-22 comes from general knowledge and is hedged; casualty figures are deliberately vague. The war-risk effects on Red Sea shipping and on refugee flows toward Sudan are estimates taken from the editors' connections, not measured data. Many Ethiopian and Eritrean claims come from the warring parties and were not independently verified. No chart is included because we lack a sourced numeric series.
